◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Bad data models are the #1 reason analytics teams burn out. Queries take 10 minutes, dashboards lie, and every new question requires a SQL archaeologist. Good modeling is the difference between a team that ships and a team that drowns. This is the single highest-leverage skill in analytics engineering.

What modeling means in analytics

Data modeling in analytics means transforming raw operational data into structures designed for asking business questions. It's not about storing data — that's already done. It's about shaping data so questions become easy.

DATA MODELING = QUESTION-FRIENDLY DATA
Raw data is shaped for the SYSTEM that created it.
Modeled data is shaped for the QUESTIONS people will ask.

Modeling is the bridge between operational reality and business insight.

OLTP vs OLAP

Two fundamentally different world views:

OLTP (Online Transaction Processing) Optimized for fast WRITES of single rows. Powers apps. Examples: Postgres backing a SaaS app, Stripe's payment ledger.
OLAP (Online Analytical Processing) Optimized for fast READS of millions of rows. Powers analytics. Examples: Snowflake, BigQuery, Databricks.

An OLTP database stores data in highly normalized form — split into many small tables to avoid update anomalies. An OLAP warehouse stores data denormalized — wider tables, fewer joins, optimized for scanning.

Why raw data is hard to query

Raw operational data fights you in three ways:

  1. Too normalized — Customer info lives across 8 tables (customers, addresses, phones, emails, preferences, ...). Every analytical question requires 8 joins.
  2. Wrong grain — Order data has one row per item per order, but you want one row per order for revenue analysis.
  3. Unstable schemas — Source columns get renamed, dropped, or repurposed by the app team without warning.
▸ THE PAIN OF RAW DATA

To answer "total revenue by customer segment last quarter" from raw OLTP data, you might need to:

SELECT s.name, SUM(oi.quantity * oi.price)
FROM customers c
JOIN customer_segments cs ON c.id = cs.customer_id AND cs.is_current
JOIN segments s ON cs.segment_id = s.id
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id
JOIN products p ON oi.product_id = p.id
LEFT JOIN refunds r ON r.order_id = o.id
WHERE o.created_at >= '2025-Q4-start'
  AND o.status = 'completed'
  AND r.id IS NULL  -- exclude refunded
GROUP BY s.name;

Modeled data turns this into SELECT segment, SUM(revenue) FROM fct_orders WHERE quarter = '2025Q4' GROUP BY segment. Same answer, 1/10th the SQL.

Signs of a bad model

  • Queries require 5+ JOINs for basic questions
  • Same metric calculated differently in different reports
  • "Don't trust that dashboard" — institutional knowledge of which numbers are reliable
  • Long-running queries (5+ min) for routine analysis
  • Mystery columns — no one remembers what flag_x means
  • Inconsistent grain across reports
  • Source schema changes break everything

Signs of a good model

  • Common questions = simple queries (one table, one filter, one group by)
  • One definition per metric — revenue means the same thing everywhere
  • Documented columns — clear descriptions, units, lineage
  • Consistent grain within a fact table
  • Stable interface — source changes don't ripple into marts
  • Tests catch issues before users do

The analytics engineer's job

Sit between raw data (source systems) and consumers (analysts, BI tools, ML, executives). Build the layers that translate one to the other. Modeling is the core craft.

◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Data modeling = shaping raw data for the questions that will be asked
  • OLTP optimizes for writes (apps); OLAP optimizes for reads (analytics)
  • Raw data is too normalized, wrong grain, and unstable for analytics
  • Bad models: many joins, inconsistent metrics, mystery columns, slow queries
  • Good models: simple queries, one metric definition, stable interface, documented
  • Analytics engineers bridge raw data and consumers via modeled layers

Definitions to own: a DIMENSION is descriptive context — the who, what, where, when around a fact. And a good model has: a clear grain, descriptive names, tests, and documentation — all four, not just working SQL.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The normalization spectrum determines how easy your data is to update vs to query. OLTP needs heavy normalization for write integrity. Analytics needs denormalization for read speed. Knowing where on the spectrum to land — and when — is half the modeling battle.

What normalization means

Normalization is the process of organizing tables so each piece of information lives in exactly one place. The opposite — denormalization — duplicates data across tables to speed up reads.

THE TRADE-OFF
Normalized: easy updates, slow queries, complex joins
Denormalized: hard updates, fast queries, wide flat tables

OLTP picks normalized (writes win).
OLAP picks denormalized (reads win).

The normal forms (1NF, 2NF, 3NF)

Formal normalization rules from relational theory. You don't need to memorize all five; understand the first three:

1NF: Atomic values, no repeating groups

# NOT 1NF — multiple values in one cell
| customer_id | phone_numbers              |
| 1           | 555-1234, 555-5678         |
| 2           | 555-9999                   |

# 1NF — each value gets its own row
| customer_id | phone_number |
| 1           | 555-1234     |
| 1           | 555-5678     |
| 2           | 555-9999     |

2NF: 1NF + no partial dependencies on composite keys

# NOT 2NF — product_name depends only on product_id (part of composite PK)
order_items table:
| order_id | product_id | quantity | product_name |    ← product_name doesn't depend on order_id
| 1        | A          | 3        | Widget       |
| 1        | B          | 1        | Gadget       |
| 2        | A          | 2        | Widget       |    ← duplicated!

# 2NF — split into separate tables
order_items: (order_id, product_id, quantity)
products:    (product_id, product_name)

3NF: 2NF + no transitive dependencies

# NOT 3NF — city depends on zip, not on customer_id
customers:
| customer_id | name  | zip   | city    | state |
| 1           | Alice | 10001 | NYC     | NY    |
| 2           | Bob   | 10001 | NYC     | NY    |    ← redundant zip → city

# 3NF — split out zip-to-city mapping
customers:  (customer_id, name, zip)
zip_codes:  (zip, city, state)

Most production OLTP databases aim for 3NF — enough to avoid most update anomalies without going crazy.

Why OLTP databases normalize

  1. Update anomalies — change a product name in one place, not 1000
  2. Insertion anomalies — add a new customer without needing order data
  3. Deletion anomalies — delete an order without losing customer info
  4. Storage efficiency — historically expensive when disks cost real money

Why analytics denormalizes

  1. Query simplicity — fewer JOINs in every analytical query
  2. Query speed — modern columnar warehouses scan flat wide tables fast
  3. Cheap storage — Snowflake/BigQuery storage is essentially free
  4. Read-heavy workloads — updates happen via batched rebuilds, not individual writes
  5. Compression — columnar warehouses compress duplicated values very efficiently
★ THE COLUMNAR ADVANTAGE

In a row-store database, denormalizing wastes space (every row has all columns). In a columnar warehouse, a column with duplicated values compresses to nearly nothing. So denormalization is virtually free in modern warehouses — capture that win.

Where to land on the spectrum

Source data Whatever shape the source system uses (usually 3NF)
Staging (stg_) Match source 1:1 — light renames, casts, no logic
Intermediate (int_) Joins, transforms, business logic — flatter than staging
Marts (fct_/dim_) Highly denormalized — wide dimensions, flat facts
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Denormalizing for analytics
# Source (3NF):
# orders         (order_id, customer_id, order_date, status)
# order_items    (order_id, product_id, quantity, unit_price)
# products       (product_id, name, category_id)
# product_cats   (category_id, category_name)
# customers      (customer_id, name, segment_id, ...)
# customer_segs  (segment_id, segment_name)

# Mart (denormalized) — fct_order_items:
SELECT
    oi.order_id,
    oi.product_id,
    o.order_date,
    o.customer_id,
    c.name AS customer_name,            -- flattened from customers
    cs.segment_name AS customer_segment, -- flattened across 2 joins
    p.name AS product_name,             -- flattened from products
    pc.category_name AS product_category, -- flattened across 2 joins
    oi.quantity,
    oi.unit_price,
    oi.quantity * oi.unit_price AS line_revenue  -- pre-computed
FROM order_items oi
JOIN orders o ON ...
JOIN customers c ON ...
JOIN customer_segs cs ON ...
JOIN products p ON ...
JOIN product_cats pc ON ...

# Analyst queries now:
SELECT customer_segment, SUM(line_revenue)
FROM fct_order_items
WHERE order_date >= '2025-10-01'
GROUP BY customer_segment;
# Zero JOINs. Fast.
◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Normalization eliminates redundancy by splitting tables
  • 1NF: atomic values; 2NF: no partial deps; 3NF: no transitive deps
  • OLTP databases normalize to 3NF for write integrity
  • Analytics warehouses denormalize for read speed
  • Columnar storage makes duplication essentially free
  • Staging stays close to source; marts get aggressively denormalized
  • The job is moving data from source's shape to analyst's shape

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The three-layer pattern (staging → intermediate → marts) is the dominant convention in modern analytics engineering, especially in dbt. Following it makes your projects readable to anyone who's worked in dbt. Ignoring it makes your project an unmaintainable swamp.

The three layers

THE THREE-LAYER ARCHITECTURE
Staging (stg_): 1:1 with sources, lightly cleaned
Intermediate (int_): joins, business logic, prep work
Marts (fct_/dim_): consumable, denormalized, business-meaningful

Layer 1: Staging

One staging model per source table. Goal: standardize source data, not transform it.

# models/staging/stripe/stg_stripe__charges.sql

with source as (
    select * from {{ source('stripe', 'charges') }}
),

renamed as (
    select
        id              as charge_id,
        customer        as customer_id,
        amount / 100.0  as amount_usd,     -- Stripe stores cents
        currency::text  as currency,
        captured        as is_captured,
        created::timestamp as created_at,
        refunded        as is_refunded
    from source
)

select * from renamed

What staging DOES:

  • Rename columns to consistent style (snake_case, descriptive)
  • Cast types (timestamps as timestamp, IDs as text)
  • Apply simple unit conversions (cents → dollars)
  • Drop columns you'll never use

What staging DOES NOT:

  • JOIN to other tables
  • Apply business logic ("is_premium customer")
  • Aggregate or summarize
  • Pivot or reshape

Layer 2: Intermediate

Where business logic and joins happen. Often hidden from end users — these are building blocks for marts.

# models/intermediate/finance/int_orders_with_refunds.sql

with orders as (
    select * from {{ ref('stg_app__orders') }}
),

refunds as (
    select
        order_id,
        sum(amount_usd) as total_refunded_usd
    from {{ ref('stg_stripe__refunds') }}
    group by 1
)

select
    o.*,
    coalesce(r.total_refunded_usd, 0) as total_refunded_usd,
    o.amount_usd - coalesce(r.total_refunded_usd, 0) as net_revenue_usd,
    case
        when r.total_refunded_usd is not null then 'refunded'
        else o.status
    end as effective_status
from orders o
left join refunds r using (order_id)

What intermediate DOES:

  • JOINs across staging models
  • Aggregations (preparing data for marts)
  • Business logic (status derivations, segmentation)
  • Pivot/unpivot operations

Convention: prefix int_, often materialized as ephemeral (compiled into downstream queries, not stored).

Layer 3: Marts

The user-facing layer. Optimized for analysts and BI tools. Highly denormalized. Stable interface — versioned carefully.

# models/marts/finance/fct_orders.sql

select
    order_id,
    customer_id,
    order_date,
    order_date_month,
    
    -- customer dimensions denormalized in
    customer_name,
    customer_segment,
    customer_country,
    
    -- product info denormalized in
    product_id,
    product_name,
    product_category,
    
    -- measures
    amount_usd,
    total_refunded_usd,
    net_revenue_usd,
    
    -- derived flags
    effective_status,
    is_premium_customer
from {{ ref('int_orders_with_refunds') }}
join {{ ref('int_customers_enriched') }} using (customer_id)
join {{ ref('stg_app__products') }} using (product_id)

Why this pattern works

Separation of concerns Each layer has one job. Easier to test, debug, and change.
Source isolation If a source schema changes, only staging breaks. Marts are insulated.
Reusability Staging and intermediate models feed many marts.
Discoverability Anyone new can find code: stg_ for sources, fct_/dim_ for finals.
Testability Test each layer independently with appropriate tests.

Common layer violations

⚠ ANTI-PATTERNS
  • Joining sources in staging — staging should be 1:1 with sources
  • Putting business logic in staging — keep logic in intermediate
  • Referencing sources directly from marts — always go through staging
  • Querying intermediate models from BI tools — only marts are user-facing
  • Skipping intermediate when logic is non-trivial — creates unmaintainable marts

When to skip the intermediate layer

Simple marts that just renaming + joining a few staging models don't need an intermediate layer. The hierarchy is conceptual: staging → marts for simple cases, staging → intermediate → marts for complex ones. Don't add layers just because.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — A real layer flow
# Question: What's monthly revenue by customer segment?

# Sources (raw):
# - stripe.charges (raw payment data)
# - app.orders (order metadata)
# - app.customers (customer info)
# - app.customer_segments (segment assignments)

# Layer 1 — Staging:
# stg_stripe__charges      → rename, cast, normalize
# stg_app__orders          → ...
# stg_app__customers       → ...
# stg_app__customer_segments → ...

# Layer 2 — Intermediate:
# int_orders_with_refunds  → join orders + charges, compute net
# int_customers_enriched   → join customers + segments

# Layer 3 — Marts:
# fct_orders               → wide table, all order info + customer denormalized
# dim_customers            → wide customer dim with segment info

# Analyst query:
SELECT
    DATE_TRUNC('month', order_date) AS month,
    customer_segment,
    SUM(net_revenue_usd) AS revenue
FROM fct_orders
WHERE order_date >= '2025-01-01'
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2;
◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Three layers: staging → intermediate → marts
  • Staging (stg_): 1:1 with sources, light cleaning only
  • Intermediate (int_): joins, business logic, building blocks
  • Marts (fct_/dim_): denormalized, user-facing, stable interface
  • Each layer has one job — separation of concerns
  • Source schema changes only ripple to staging — marts insulated
  • Skip intermediate for simple marts; use it when logic is complex
  • BI tools and analysts only query marts

Mart conventions: naming — fct_<event> for facts, dim_<entity> for dimensions. Materialization — marts build as TABLE or INCREMENTAL for BI performance (views are for staging).

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Facts and dimensions are the most important concepts in analytical data modeling. Every dashboard, KPI, and report you'll ever build sits on this foundation. Get the distinction wrong and your models will fight you forever. Get it right and queries become obvious.

The Kimball framework

Ralph Kimball developed dimensional modeling in the 1990s as a pragmatic way to structure analytical databases. It's now the dominant approach in analytics. The core idea: organize data into facts (what happened) and dimensions (the context of what happened).

FACTS vs DIMENSIONS
Fact: a measurable business event (an order, a click, a payment)
Dimension: the context describing the event (which customer? which product? when? where?)

Fact tables

Fact tables store events — things that happened. Each row is one event. Columns are mostly numeric measures (quantity, amount, duration) plus foreign keys to dimensions.

# fct_orders — one row per order
| order_id | customer_id | product_id | date_id  | quantity | amount | discount |
| 1001     | C42         | P7         | 20250515 | 3        | 89.97  | 0        |
| 1002     | C42         | P11        | 20250515 | 1        | 19.99  | 5        |
| 1003     | C18         | P7         | 20250516 | 2        | 59.98  | 0        |

Characteristics of fact tables:

  • Tall and skinny — many rows (millions to billions), few columns
  • Mostly numeric — measures (sums, counts, durations)
  • FK to dimensions — every fact row connects to multiple dimensions
  • Append-only mostly — events don't usually change after the fact

Dimension tables

Dimension tables store descriptive context — the nouns of your business. Each row is one customer, one product, one date.

# dim_customers — one row per customer
| customer_id | name          | segment    | country | signup_date | is_premium |
| C42         | Alice Johnson | enterprise | USA     | 2024-01-15  | TRUE       |
| C18         | Bob Smith     | small_biz  | UK      | 2025-03-22  | FALSE      |

# dim_products — one row per product
| product_id | name        | category    | brand     | unit_price |
| P7         | Widget Pro  | electronics | Acme      | 29.99      |
| P11        | Gadget Max  | electronics | TechCo    | 19.99      |

# dim_date — one row per date (continuous)
| date_id  | date       | year | quarter | month | day_of_week | is_weekend |
| 20250515 | 2025-05-15 | 2025 | Q2      | 5     | Thursday    | FALSE      |
| 20250516 | 2025-05-16 | 2025 | Q2      | 5     | Friday      | FALSE      |

Characteristics of dimension tables:

  • Wide and short — many columns describing each entity, fewer rows
  • Mostly text + dates — descriptive attributes
  • Slowly changing — customer info changes occasionally, not constantly
  • Used to filter and group — "by region", "by month", "by segment"

Identifying facts vs dimensions in real data

Event Fact table Dimensions
Customer places an order fct_orders customer, product, date, store
User clicks a button fct_events user, page, device, date
Subscription renews fct_subscriptions customer, plan, billing_period
Driver completes a delivery fct_deliveries driver, customer, restaurant, date, location
Patient takes a medication fct_medication_events patient, medication, prescriber, date, location

The fact-vs-dimension test

★ A QUICK HEURISTIC

Ask: "Does this answer the question (fact) or describe the context (dimension)?"

  • "Total revenue last month" → fact (a measure)
  • "Customer's home country" → dimension (an attribute)
  • "Order amount" → fact
  • "Product category" → dimension
  • "How many orders" → fact (count of events)
  • "Order status" → dimension (descriptive attribute of an order — could be a fact attribute though, see grain)

A simple query pattern

The whole point of fact/dim modeling is making this query trivial:

# Standard analytical query shape:
SELECT
    <dimension attribute(s)>,
    <aggregation of fact measure(s)>
FROM fact_table f
JOIN dim_table d ON f.dim_id = d.dim_id
WHERE <dimension filter>
GROUP BY <dimension attribute(s)>;

# Example: Revenue by product category, last quarter
SELECT
    p.category,
    SUM(o.amount) AS total_revenue
FROM fct_orders o
JOIN dim_products p ON o.product_id = p.product_id
JOIN dim_date d ON o.date_id = d.date_id
WHERE d.year = 2025 AND d.quarter = 'Q1'

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Grain is the most important question to answer when building a fact table. Get the grain wrong and your numbers will be subtly broken — double-counting, missing rows, or computing the wrong thing. Kimball himself called grain "the most important step" in dimensional modeling.

What grain means

The grain of a fact table is the level of detail represented by one row. It answers: "What does a single row in this fact table represent?"

DECLARE THE GRAIN EXPLICITLY
Before you write any SQL, write the grain in one sentence:

"One row in fct_orders represents one order."
"One row in fct_order_items represents one item within one order."
"One row in fct_page_views represents one pageview by one user."

Get this right first. Everything else flows from it.

Choosing the right grain

Always choose the most atomic grain possible for the business event. You can aggregate up to summaries, but you can't drill down past the grain you stored.

Business event Atomic grain (best) Bad grain
E-commerce orders One row per order item One row per order (loses item detail)
Web analytics One row per pageview One row per session (loses page detail)
Subscription billing One row per invoice line item One row per invoice (loses line breakdown)
Patient visits One row per procedure One row per visit (loses procedure detail)

The mixed-grain disaster

The classic modeling mistake: a fact table where different rows mean different things. Example:

# BAD — mixed grain
fct_orders:
| id  | order_id | item_id | amount | row_type      |
| 1   | 1001     | NULL    | 89.97  | order_total   |    ← one grain: per order
| 2   | 1001     | A       | 29.99  | order_item    |    ← different grain: per item!
| 3   | 1001     | B       | 19.99  | order_item    |
| 4   | 1001     | C       | 39.99  | order_item    |
| 5   | 1002     | A       | 29.99  | order_item    |
| 6   | 1002     | NULL    | 29.99  | order_total   |

# What's SUM(amount)? 269.93 — but actual revenue is only 119.96.
# Double-counted because rows mix grains.
⚠ NEVER MIX GRAINS

If you have both order-level and item-level data, build two fact tables: fct_orders (per order) and fct_order_items (per item). Don't shove them into one.

Declared grain in schema.yml

Always document the grain in dbt schema.yml — it's the single most important piece of model documentation:

# models/marts/schema.yml
models:
  - name: fct_orders
    description: |
      Order-level fact table. One row per completed order.
      Grain: one order. Order_id is unique.
    columns:
      - name: order_id
        description: Unique order identifier
        tests:
          - unique
          - not_null
      - name: amount_usd
        description: Total order amount in USD (sum of line items)

  - name: fct_order_items
    description: |
      Order-item-level fact table. One row per line item per order.
      Grain: one (order_id, line_item_id) pair.
    columns:
      - name: order_item_id
        description: Surrogate key — unique per row
        tests:
          - unique
          - not_null
      - name: order_id
        description: FK to fct_orders
        tests:
          - relationships:
              to: ref('fct_orders')
              field: order_id

Tests verify the grain holds:

  • unique on the grain key (or composite of grain keys)
  • not_null on grain keys
  • Row count checks (sanity bounds)
  • dbt_utils.unique_combination_of_columns for composite grains
# Composite grain test
- name: fct_order_items
  tests:
    - dbt_utils.unique_combination_of_columns:
        combination_of_columns:
          - order_id
          - line_item_id

Grain and aggregation

Once grain is set, all aggregations roll up from there:

# Starting from fct_order_items (per item), you can:

# Sum to order level
SELECT order_id, SUM(line_amount) AS order_total
FROM fct_order_items
GROUP BY order_id;

# Sum to day level
SELECT order_date, SUM(line_amount) AS daily_revenue
FROM fct_order_items
GROUP BY order_date;

# Sum to customer level
SELECT customer_id, SUM(line_amount) AS lifetime_value
FROM fct_order_items
GROUP BY customer_id;

# ALL of these are valid because grain is atomic (item level).
# You can roll up to ANY higher level by aggregating.

Sometimes source data is already aggregated (e.g., third-party API returns daily totals). Accept the grain you have but document it explicitly:

# Business: SaaS company; customers have subscriptions; subs have billing periods

# OPTION A: One row per subscription
# - Loses billing period detail (renewal history)
# - Bad: can't ask "MRR by month"

# OPTION B: One row per subscription per month
# - Captures monthly MRR, churn, expansion
# - Standard SaaS grain

# OPTION C: One row per invoice
# - Captures actual billing events
# - Better for finance reporting

# Reality: you usually want BOTH:
# - fct_subscription_periods (grain: sub × month) for MRR analysis
# - fct_invoices (grain: per invoice) for finance

# Document each clearly:
fct_subscription_periods:
  grain: one (subscription_id, year_month) pair
  use_for: MRR, churn, expansion analysis

  • Grain = what one row in a fact table represents
  • Declare grain in plain English BEFORE writing SQL
  • Always choose the most atomic grain — you can aggregate up, not drill down
  • Mixed grain = double counting, broken metrics
  • Document grain in schema.yml descriptions
  • Test grain with unique + not_null (or unique_combination_of_columns for composite)
  • Build multiple fact tables if you need different grains

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Not every numeric column in a fact table can be summed. Sum the wrong measures across the wrong dimensions and you get nonsense numbers. Kimball categorized measures into additive, semi-additive, and non-additive — each requires different aggregation rules. Get this right and your dashboards stop lying.

The three classes of measures

ADDITIVITY CLASSES
Additive: can SUM across any dimension. Most measures.
Semi-additive: can SUM across some dimensions but NOT time. Balances, inventory.
Non-additive: can't SUM across any dimension. Ratios, percentages, averages.

Additive measures

The easy case: you can sum these across any dimension and get a meaningful answer.

# Sales amount is additive
SELECT SUM(amount) FROM fct_orders;                            -- total revenue
SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) FROM fct_orders GROUP BY 1;    -- by customer
SELECT order_date, SUM(amount) FROM fct_orders GROUP BY 1;     -- by date
SELECT product_id, SUM(amount) FROM fct_orders GROUP BY 1;     -- by product
SELECT customer_id, product_id, SUM(amount) FROM fct_orders GROUP BY 1,2;  -- both

# All produce correct answers. Amount is additive.

Common additive measures: revenue, quantity, count, duration, units sold, clicks, page views.

Semi-additive measures

The trap: balances, levels, and stocks can be summed across most dimensions but not across time. Summing balances across days produces nonsense.

# fct_account_balances_daily
| account_id | snapshot_date | balance |
| A1         | 2025-05-14    | 1000    |
| A1         | 2025-05-15    | 1200    |    ← deposited 200
| A1         | 2025-05-16    | 1200    |
| A2         | 2025-05-14    | 500     |
| A2         | 2025-05-15    | 500     |
| A2         | 2025-05-16    | 800     |

# WRONG: sum across time
SELECT SUM(balance) FROM fct_account_balances_daily;
# Returns 5200, but no such concept exists ("total balance" across days is meaningless)

# RIGHT: sum across accounts AT a point in time
SELECT SUM(balance) FROM fct_account_balances_daily 
WHERE snapshot_date = '2025-05-16';
# Returns 2000 — total balance across all accounts on that day

# RIGHT: average balance over time per account
SELECT account_id, AVG(balance) FROM fct_account_balances_daily
GROUP BY account_id;
# Average — meaningful temporal aggregation

Common semi-additive measures:

  • Account balance — sum across accounts; average over time
  • Inventory level — sum across warehouses; average/min/max over time
  • MRR — sum across customers; can't sum across months
  • Headcount — sum across departments; can't sum across days
  • Active users — sum within a period; can't add periods
⚠ THE CLASSIC BUG

Dashboards display "Total MRR" by summing monthly MRR across 12 months → reports look 12× higher than reality. Always think: can I sum this across time? If not, use AVG, MAX, or filter to a point in time.

Non-additive measures

Ratios, percentages, averages — cannot be summed across any dimension. Trying to sum them is always wrong.

# fct_orders has unit_price (non-additive!)
# unit_price = amount / quantity per row

# WRONG: sum unit prices
SELECT product_id, SUM(unit_price) FROM fct_orders GROUP BY 1;
# Meaningless

# RIGHT: average unit price (weighted or unweighted)
SELECT product_id, AVG(unit_price) FROM fct_orders GROUP BY 1;
# Unweighted average

# RIGHT: re-compute the ratio from additive measures
SELECT product_id, SUM(amount) / SUM(quantity) AS weighted_avg_price
FROM fct_orders GROUP BY 1;
# Weighted by volume — usually what you want

Common non-additive measures: prices, rates, percentages, averages, ratios, distinct counts.

The fix for non-additive: store the ingredients

Instead of storing the ratio, store its components and compute on-the-fly:

# BAD — pre-compute the ratio
fct_orders:
| order_id | unit_price |    ← non-additive
| 1001     | 29.99      |
| 1002     | 19.99      |

# GOOD — store components
fct_orders:
| order_id | amount  | quantity |    ← both additive
| 1001     | 89.97   | 3        |
| 1002     | 19.99   | 1        |

# Compute ratios in queries:
SELECT product_id, SUM(amount) / SUM(quantity) AS avg_price
FROM fct_orders GROUP BY 1;

Counts vs distinct counts

A subtle but critical distinction:

# COUNT(*) is additive
# COUNT(DISTINCT x) is NOT additive

# Example: distinct customers per day
| day | distinct_customers |
| Mon | 100                |
| Tue | 120                |
| Wed | 110                |

# Can you sum to get "weekly distinct customers"?
# NO — same customer might appear multiple days
# Correct answer = count distinct across all 3 days (could be 200, not 330)

# Pre-compute distinct counts at the grain you need them.
# Or store user-day rows and compute distinct in the query.

Documenting additivity in schema.yml

columns:
  - name: amount_usd
    description: Order amount in USD. ADDITIVE across all dimensions.

  - name: balance_usd
    description: |
      Account balance in USD. SEMI-ADDITIVE.
      Sum across accounts; AVG or last-value over time.

  - name: gross_margin_pct
    description: |
      Gross margin as a percentage. NON-ADDITIVE.
      Cannot be summed. Use weighted average: SUM(gross_margin) / SUM(revenue).

| customer_id | year_month | mrr |
| C42         | 2025-03    | 29  |
| C42         | 2025-04    | 99  |
| C42         | 2025-05    | 99  |

  • COUNT(*) is additive; COUNT(DISTINCT) is not
  • Document additivity in schema.yml column descriptions

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Every fact and dimension table needs a primary key. The choice between using the source system's natural keys vs generated surrogate keys affects performance, stability, and how easy your warehouse is to evolve. The convention in modern analytics: use surrogate keys.

Natural vs surrogate keys

KEY TYPES
Natural key: identifier from the source system (e.g., email, SKU, order_number)
Surrogate key: meaningless ID generated specifically for your warehouse (often a hash or sequence)

Why surrogate keys

Surrogate keys decouple your warehouse from source system quirks:

  • Source key changes — sources sometimes change identifier formats. Surrogate stays stable.
  • Source key reuse — sometimes IDs get recycled. Surrogate gives uniqueness.
  • Composite natural keys — natural key might be 3-4 columns. Surrogate collapses to one.
  • Type consistency — surrogate is usually a fixed type (int or string hash).
  • SCD type 2 — same business entity can have multiple versions (rows). Surrogate distinguishes them.

Generating surrogate keys

Two common patterns in dbt:

# Pattern 1: hash the natural key columns
# Uses dbt_utils.generate_surrogate_key

select
    {{ dbt_utils.generate_surrogate_key(['customer_id', 'effective_date']) }} as customer_sk,
    customer_id,
    ...
from staged

# Result: customer_sk is a deterministic hash, e.g.:
# 'a7f3e2d9c8b1e4f6...'  (md5 hash, 32 chars)

# Pattern 2: sequence number (less common in dbt)
select
    row_number() over (order by customer_id) as customer_sk,
    customer_id,
    ...
from staged

Hash-based surrogate keys

The dominant approach in dbt. dbt_utils.generate_surrogate_key creates an MD5 hash of the given columns:

# Why hash-based wins:
# - Deterministic: same inputs always give same hash
# - Stable across runs: doesn't depend on row order
# - Distributed: no central sequence needed
# - Composite-friendly: hash any number of columns
# - Idempotent: rebuilding produces same keys

# Define keys in models:

# Simple dim (one natural key)
{{ dbt_utils.generate_surrogate_key(['customer_id']) }} as customer_sk

# SCD2 dim (key + effective date)
{{ dbt_utils.generate_surrogate_key(['customer_id', 'valid_from']) }} as customer_sk

# Composite natural key (order_id + line_number)
{{ dbt_utils.generate_surrogate_key(['order_id', 'line_number']) }} as order_item_sk

Keep the natural key too

Surrogate keys are for the warehouse; natural keys are for humans and source-traceability. Always keep both:

# dim_customers
| customer_sk      | customer_id  | name  | ... |    ← surrogate AND natural
| 'a7f3e2d9c8b1'   | 'C42'        | Alice |     |
| '5e9c4a2f8b3d'   | 'C18'        | Bob   |     |

# customer_sk: primary key, foreign keys reference this
# customer_id: traceability to source, debug queries

Foreign keys reference surrogates

# fct_orders references dim_customers via surrogate
| order_id | customer_sk      | amount |
| 1001     | 'a7f3e2d9c8b1'   | 89.97  |    ← matches dim_customers.customer_sk
| 1002     | 'a7f3e2d9c8b1'   | 19.99  |
| 1003     | '5e9c4a2f8b3d'   | 59.98  |

# In the fact's model:
select
    order_id,
    {{ dbt_utils.generate_surrogate_key(['customer_id']) }} as customer_sk,
    amount,
    ...
from staged_orders

Date keys: special case

Date dimensions usually use a meaningful integer key like YYYYMMDD rather than a hash. Easier to debug, sort, and reason about:

# dim_date
| date_id  | date       | year | quarter | month |
| 20250515 | 2025-05-15 | 2025 | Q2      | 5     |
| 20250516 | 2025-05-16 | 2025 | Q2      | 5     |

# fct_orders references date_id (integer)
| order_id | order_date_id | ... |
| 1001     | 20250515      |     |

# Easy to filter:
WHERE order_date_id BETWEEN 20250101 AND 20251231

# Two common conventions:
# 1. YYYYMMDD integer (e.g., 20250515)
# 2. Actual DATE type (e.g., '2025-05-15')
# Both work; pick one and be consistent.

Why NOT to use surrogate keys

Sometimes natural keys are fine:

  • Small project — overhead doesn't justify it
  • Natural key is stable, unique, and atomic — already perfect
  • You're not doing SCD2 — no need to distinguish versions
  • Tight integration with source systems — natural keys are the contract

For most analytics warehouses though: use surrogate keys by default.

Testing surrogate keys

  columns:
    - name: customer_sk
      description: Surrogate primary key
      tests:
        - unique
        - not_null

    - name: customer_id
      description: Natural key from source
      tests:
        - unique           # in SCD1; remove for SCD2
        - not_null

- name: fct_orders
  columns:

        - relationships:

  • Default to surrogate keys: stability, type consistency, SCD2 support
  • dbt convention: hash-based via dbt_utils.generate_surrogate_key
  • Hashes are deterministic, idempotent, distributed-friendly
  • Always keep the natural key alongside surrogate for traceability
  • Foreign keys reference surrogate keys (not natural)
  • Date dimensions often use YYYYMMDD integer keys for readability
  • Test surrogate keys with unique + not_null

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Customers change segments. Products change categories. Employees change titles. The question of how to track these changes — Slowly Changing Dimensions (SCD) — is THE classic data warehouse problem. Kimball defined seven types; you'll use three of them (Type 0, 1, 2) constantly.

The SCD problem

When a dimension's attribute changes, what do you do? Three main strategies:

THE THREE PRACTICAL SCD TYPES
Type 0: Never change. Original value frozen forever.
Type 1: Overwrite. Current value only. No history.
Type 2: Track history. New row per change with valid_from/valid_to.
Type 3: Limited history (current + previous columns).

SCD Type 0 — Retain Original

The original value never changes, even if the source updates. Used for unchanging facts about an entity.

# Example: customer's original signup date or acquisition channel
| customer_id | original_signup_date | original_acquisition_channel |
| C42         | 2024-01-15           | google_ads                   |
| C18         | 2025-03-22           | organic_search               |

# If source's signup_date is later corrected, we IGNORE the change
# The original value is the truth we care about

Common Type 0 attributes: original signup date, first purchase date, acquisition channel.

SCD Type 1 — Overwrite

The most common: just update the row with the latest value. No history retained.

# Before: customer was in 'small_biz' segment
| customer_id | segment   | email           | country |
| C42         | small_biz | alice@old.com   | USA     |

# Customer upgrades + changes email
# After Type 1 update:
| customer_id | segment    | email           | country |
| C42         | enterprise | alice@new.com   | USA     |

# History of old segment is LOST

Use Type 1 when:

  • History of the change doesn't matter for analysis
  • You just need to know "what's true right now"
  • Simple corrections (typo fixes, formatting)

SCD Type 2 — Add New Row

The powerhouse. When an attribute changes, you insert a new row with a new effective date range. The old row's valid_to closes; a new row opens.

# Customer C42 starts in small_biz segment on 2024-01-15
# Upgrades to enterprise on 2025-04-15

dim_customers (SCD2):
| customer_sk | customer_id | segment    | valid_from | valid_to   | is_current |
| sk_001      | C42         | small_biz  | 2024-01-15 | 2025-04-15 | false      |
| sk_002      | C42         | enterprise | 2025-04-15 | 9999-12-31 | true       |

# Now you can answer historical questions:
# "Was C42 enterprise on 2025-02-01?" → No, small_biz at that time
# "What was C42's segment when they placed order O123?"
#    → JOIN order_date BETWEEN valid_from AND valid_to

SCD2 columns (standard set):

  • valid_from / effective_date — when this version became active
  • valid_to / end_date — when this version stopped (often 9999-12-31 for current)
  • is_current — boolean for fast "show me current" filtering
  • version (optional) — incrementing version number per business key

Joining facts to SCD2 dimensions

# For "as-was" analysis (segment as of the order date)
SELECT 
    c.segment,
    SUM(o.amount) AS revenue
FROM fct_orders o
JOIN dim_customers c 
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
    AND o.order_date BETWEEN c.valid_from AND c.valid_to
GROUP BY c.segment;

# For "current state" analysis (latest segment, regardless of when ordered)
SELECT
    c.segment,
    SUM(o.amount) AS revenue
FROM fct_orders o
JOIN dim_customers c 
    ON c.customer_id = o.customer_id
    AND c.is_current = true
GROUP BY c.segment;
★ TWO COMMON ANALYSIS LENSES

"As-was" = what was true at the time. "Current state" = what's true now. Different questions, different joins. SCD2 lets you answer both. Document which is intended in your reports.

SCD Type 3 — Add New Column

Track just the previous value alongside the current. Limited history but no row explosion.

# dim_customers (SCD3 on segment)
| customer_id | current_segment | previous_segment | segment_changed_at |
| C42         | enterprise      | small_biz        | 2025-04-15         |
| C18         | small_biz       | NULL             | NULL               |

# Use when:
# - You care about the most recent change but not all history
# - You want one row per customer (simpler joins)
# - Two values is enough context

Less common than Type 1 or 2. Sometimes useful for slow-moving attributes where you only care about "current vs previous."

SCD Type 2 in dbt: snapshots

dbt has native support for SCD2 via snapshots:

# snapshots/customers_snapshot.sql

{% snapshot customers_snapshot %}

{{
    config(
      target_schema='snapshots',
      unique_key='customer_id',
      strategy='check',
      check_cols=['segment', 'email', 'country'],
    )
}}

select * from {{ source('app', 'customers') }}

{% endsnapshot %}

# Run dbt snapshot daily; dbt automatically:
# - Detects changes in check_cols
# - Inserts new rows with dbt_valid_from / dbt_valid_to
# - Closes out previous rows
# - Adds dbt_scd_id (unique per version)

# Then in your dim model:
select
    {{ dbt_utils.generate_surrogate_key(['customer_id', 'dbt_valid_from']) }} as customer_sk,
    customer_id,
    segment, email, country,
    dbt_valid_from as valid_from,
    coalesce(dbt_valid_to, '9999-12-31') as valid_to,
    dbt_valid_to is null as is_current
from {{ ref('customers_snapshot') }}

Choosing the right SCD type per attribute

You don't pick one SCD type per dimension — you pick per attribute. A single dim table can mix types:

Attribute Type Why
customer_id — (key) Never changes
name Type 1 Corrections; history not meaningful
email Type 1 Just track current
segment Type 2 Need to know "as-was" segment for old orders
country Type 2 Customer moves; historical attribution matters
signup_date Type 0 The original — should never change
lifetime_value Type 1 Always recompute; no history needed

SCD Type 6 is the hybrid of Types 1, 2 and 3 — the name comes from 1+2+3 (which is also 1×2×3). Each row carries the historical value (Type 2), a column holding the current value overwritten in place (Type 1), and a previous-value column (Type 3), so you can report on the fact either as-it-was or as-it-is-now without a second join.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Beyond standard dimensions, Kimball described special patterns for tricky scenarios: junk dimensions (for flag combos), role-playing dimensions (one dim used multiple ways), and bridge dimensions (for many-to-many). Knowing these patterns lets you handle complex models without resorting to ugly workarounds.

Junk dimensions

Sometimes you have a bunch of low-cardinality flags or codes that don't fit anywhere else. Rather than scatter them across fact tables or create a dim per flag, combine them into a junk dimension.

# Without junk dim — many flags clutter the fact table:
fct_orders:
| order_id | customer_id | is_gift | is_priority | is_recurring | shipping_method | ... |

# These flags have:
# - Low cardinality (boolean or small enum)
# - No natural home
# - Often used together

# With junk dim — collapse into a single dim:
dim_order_attributes:
| order_attr_sk | is_gift | is_priority | is_recurring | shipping_method  |
| 1             | false   | false       | false        | standard         |
| 2             | true    | false       | false        | standard         |
| 3             | false   | true        | false        | overnight        |
| 4             | false   | false       | true         | standard         |
| 5             | true    | true        | false        | overnight        |
... (one row per realized combination)

# fct_orders now:
| order_id | customer_id | order_attr_sk | ... |
| 1001     | C42         | 5             |     |

Use junk dimensions when:

  • Multiple low-cardinality flags exist that often appear together
  • Each flag alone doesn't justify its own dimension
  • Combinations are limited (a few hundred max)
  • You want a cleaner fact table

Role-playing dimensions

When the same dimension is used multiple ways in one fact, it's role-playing. The most common: dim_date used as order_date, ship_date, delivery_date, refund_date.

# fct_orders with multiple date roles
| order_id | order_date_id | ship_date_id | delivery_date_id | customer_id |
| 1001     | 20250515      | 20250516     | 20250519         | C42         |
| 1002     | 20250515      | 20250517     | NULL             | C42         |

# All three date_ids reference the same dim_date table
# But each plays a DIFFERENT ROLE in the order's lifecycle

# Joining with all three roles:
SELECT
    o.order_id,
    od.date AS order_date,
    sd.date AS ship_date,
    dd.date AS delivery_date,
    sd.date - od.date AS days_to_ship,
    dd.date - sd.date AS days_in_transit
FROM fct_orders o
JOIN dim_date od ON o.order_date_id = od.date_id
LEFT JOIN dim_date sd ON o.ship_date_id = sd.date_id
LEFT JOIN dim_date dd ON o.delivery_date_id = dd.date_id;

Two ways to handle role-playing dims:

Approach A: Aliased joins One physical dim_date table; aliased as od, sd, dd in queries (above example)
Approach B: View per role Create dim_order_date, dim_ship_date views over the same dim_date; cleaner BI semantics 
# Approach B example — create role-named views in dbt:
# models/marts/dim_order_date.sql
select 
    date_id as order_date_id,
    date as order_date,
    year as order_year,
    month as order_month,
    quarter as order_quarter
from {{ ref('dim_date') }}

# Similar for dim_ship_date, dim_delivery_date
# Now BI users see semantically named dims

Bridge dimensions (many-to-many)

Sometimes one fact row relates to many dimension values. Example: an order can have multiple promo codes applied. A patient can have multiple diagnoses.

# Order 1001 has promo codes "SUMMER25", "FREESHIP", "VIP"
# Storing as columns doesn't scale.

# Use a bridge table:

dim_promotions:
| promo_id | code      | type     | discount_pct |
| P1       | SUMMER25  | percent  | 25           |
| P2       | FREESHIP  | shipping | 0            |
| P3       | VIP       | percent  | 10           |

bridge_order_promotions:
| order_id | promo_id |
| 1001     | P1       |
| 1001     | P2       |
| 1001     | P3       |
| 1002     | P1       |

fct_orders:
| order_id | customer_id | amount |
| 1001     | C42         | 89.97  |

# Query promo usage:
SELECT 
    p.type,
    COUNT(DISTINCT b.order_id) AS orders_using
FROM dim_promotions p
JOIN bridge_order_promotions b USING (promo_id)
GROUP BY p.type;
⚠ BRIDGE GOTCHAS
  • Summing revenue across promotions DOUBLE-COUNTS if you JOIN through the bridge
  • Always think about cardinality when joining
  • Consider weighting (e.g., split revenue 1/N across N promos) if needed

Mini-dimensions

For dimensions with many rapidly-changing attributes, splitting off a "mini-dim" of the volatile attributes keeps the main dim stable:

# Main dim_customer (stable attributes, SCD2):
| customer_sk | customer_id | name | email | signup_date | country |

# Mini-dim dim_customer_behavior (volatile, SCD1 or own SCD2):
| behavior_sk | activity_tier | lifetime_value_tier | engagement_score | as_of_month |
| B001        | high          | premium             | 87               | 2025-05     |
| B002        | medium        | standard            | 54               | 2025-05     |

# Fact references both:
fct_orders:
| order_id | customer_sk | behavior_sk | ... |

Avoids "row explosion" when fast-changing attributes would otherwise force a new SCD2 row in the main dim every few days.

Outrigger dimensions

Sometimes a dimension references another dimension. Generally avoided (it's snowflaking), but acceptable for stable nested hierarchies:

# dim_employees references dim_managers
| employee_sk | employee_id | name  | manager_sk |
| E1          | EMP-100     | Alice | E5         |    ← refs another employee
| E2          | EMP-200     | Bob   | E5         |
| E5          | EMP-500     | Carol | NULL       |

# Useful for org hierarchies, geographic hierarchies
# But denormalize when you can
▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Complex order modeling
# E-commerce orders with realistic complexity

# Dimensions:
# - dim_customers (SCD2)
# - dim_products
# - dim_date (role-playing as order_date, ship_date, delivery_date)
# - dim_order_attributes (junk: gift?, priority?, recurring?)
# - dim_promotions
# - bridge_order_promotions (many-to-many)

# fct_orders:
| order_id | customer_sk | order_attr_sk |
|          | order_date_id | ship_date_id | delivery_date_id |
|          | amount | shipping_cost | tax |

# Now you can answer complex questions:
# "Revenue by promo type for gift orders shipped in May"
SELECT 
    p.type,
    SUM(o.amount) AS revenue
FROM fct_orders o
JOIN dim_order_attributes oa USING (order_attr_sk)
JOIN bridge_order_promotions bop USING (order_id)
JOIN dim_promotions p USING (promo_id)
JOIN dim_date sd ON o.ship_date_id = sd.date_id
WHERE oa.is_gift = true
  AND sd.month = 5 AND sd.year = 2025
GROUP BY p.type;
◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Junk dimension: combine low-cardinality flags into one dim (cleaner facts)
  • Role-playing dimension: same dim used multiple ways (especially dates)
  • Bridge table: resolves many-to-many between fact and dimension
  • Mini-dimension: split off fast-changing attributes from main dim
  • Outrigger: dim referencing another dim (snowflaking; avoid generally)
  • These patterns solve specific real problems — recognize when each fits
📊 FIGURE — a dimension key with no dimension table
🎯 EXAM TIP
Use a degenerate dimension when the key is an identifier only, with no further descriptive attributes — an order or invoice number. Building a dimension table whose sole column is its own key adds a join and stores nothing, so the id lives on the fact table instead. The moment that order acquires attributes worth storing, it stops being degenerate.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The date dimension is the single most-used table in any analytics warehouse. Every fact joins to it. Every report filters by it. A well-built date dim is the foundation of comparable, consistent time analysis. A bad one creates years of subtle bugs.

What goes in a date dimension

One row per date. Many attributes describing that date so queries can filter and group by any time perspective:

# Core attributes every dim_date needs:
date_id            -- INT YYYYMMDD or DATE
date               -- actual date
year               -- 2025
quarter            -- 'Q2' or 2
quarter_number     -- 1-4
month_number       -- 1-12
month_name         -- 'May'
month_name_short   -- 'May'
week_of_year       -- 1-53
day_of_year        -- 1-366
day_of_month       -- 1-31
day_of_week        -- 0-6 or 1-7
day_of_week_name   -- 'Wednesday'
day_of_week_short  -- 'Wed'
is_weekend         -- TRUE/FALSE
is_business_day    -- TRUE/FALSE (after holiday adjustments)
is_first_day_of_month
is_last_day_of_month

# Useful date math attributes:
prior_day          -- date - 1
prior_week         -- date - 7
prior_month        -- date - 30 (or true prior month)
prior_year         -- date - 365 (or true prior year)
next_day, next_week, next_month, next_year

# Fiscal calendar (if business uses one):
fiscal_year        -- often offset by months
fiscal_quarter
fiscal_month
fiscal_week
fiscal_period      -- depends on retail 4-4-5 etc.

# Holiday flags:
is_holiday
holiday_name        -- 'Memorial Day', NULL
is_company_holiday  -- internal company-specific
is_us_holiday
is_uk_holiday      -- per-country if multinational

Building dim_date with dbt

The cleanest way: use dbt_utils.date_spine or dbt_date.get_date_dimension:

# models/marts/dim_date.sql

-- Option 1: dbt_utils.date_spine + manual enrichment
with date_spine as (
    {{ dbt_utils.date_spine(
        datepart="day",
        start_date="cast('2015-01-01' as date)",
        end_date="cast('2035-12-31' as date)"
    ) }}
),

enriched as (
    select
        date_day as date,
        cast(to_char(date_day, 'YYYYMMDD') as int) as date_id,
        extract(year from date_day) as year,
        extract(quarter from date_day) as quarter_number,
        'Q' || extract(quarter from date_day) as quarter,
        extract(month from date_day) as month_number,
        to_char(date_day, 'Month') as month_name,
        to_char(date_day, 'Mon') as month_name_short,
        extract(week from date_day) as week_of_year,
        extract(dayofyear from date_day) as day_of_year,
        extract(day from date_day) as day_of_month,
        extract(dayofweek from date_day) as day_of_week,
        to_char(date_day, 'Day') as day_of_week_name,
        case when extract(dayofweek from date_day) in (0, 6) 
             then true else false end as is_weekend
    from date_spine
)

select * from enriched

-- Option 2: dbt_date.get_date_dimension (one line)
-- {{ dbt_date.get_date_dimension("2015-01-01", "2035-12-31") }}

Date range coverage

Build the dim_date wide enough:

  • Past start: at least the earliest date in your fact data, with a safety margin
  • Future end: at least 5-10 years out, more for long-lived schedules
  • Refresh strategy: rebuild infrequently (annually); dim_date is mostly static

Fiscal calendars

Many companies use fiscal years that don't align to calendar years (e.g., fiscal year ends April 30). Adding fiscal columns avoids messy CASE statements in every query:

# Fiscal year starts May 1:
fiscal_year_start as ('05-01')

select
    *,
    case 
        when month_number >= 5 then year 
        else year - 1 
    end as fiscal_year,
    case
        when month_number between 5 and 7 then 'Q1'
        when month_number between 8 and 10 then 'Q2'
        when month_number between 11 and 12 then 'Q3'
        when month_number between 1 and 1 then 'Q3'
        when month_number between 2 and 4 then 'Q4'
    end as fiscal_quarter,
    ...

# Now analysts query in business-aligned periods:
SELECT fiscal_year, fiscal_quarter, SUM(amount)
FROM fct_orders
JOIN dim_date USING (date_id)
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1, 2;

Holiday flags

Holiday-aware analysis is hugely valuable (retail spikes, support volume dips, etc.). Add holiday columns from a published list:

# seeds/holidays.csv
date,country,name,is_company_holiday
2025-01-01,US,New Year's Day,true
2025-05-26,US,Memorial Day,true
2025-07-04,US,Independence Day,true
2025-11-27,US,Thanksgiving,true

# Join in dim_date:
with date_base as (...),

with_holidays as (
    select 
        d.*,
        h.name as holiday_name,
        h.is_company_holiday,
        h.name is not null as is_holiday
    from date_base d
    left join {{ ref('holidays') }} h 
        on d.date = h.date and h.country = 'US'

# Now: "Sales on holidays vs non-holidays"
SELECT 
    is_holiday,
    SUM(amount) / COUNT(DISTINCT date) AS avg_daily_revenue
FROM fct_orders 
JOIN dim_date USING (date_id)
GROUP BY is_holiday;

Mark as Date Table

In Power BI, you "Mark as Date Table" so time intelligence functions work. For dbt-only stacks, no explicit marking — just naming the table dim_date and joining via a date column is enough.

Worth installing for shortcuts:

    version: [">=0.10.0", "<1.0.0"]

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Time analysis queries with a good dim_date
# With a well-built dim_date, these become trivial:

# Weekend vs weekday performance
SELECT 
    is_weekend,
    AVG(daily_revenue) AS avg_revenue
FROM (
    SELECT d.date, d.is_weekend, SUM(o.amount) AS daily_revenue
    FROM fct_orders o
    JOIN dim_date d USING (date_id)
    GROUP BY d.date, d.is_weekend
)
GROUP BY is_weekend;

# YoY comparison by month
SELECT 
    d.month_name,
    SUM(CASE WHEN d.year = 2024 THEN o.amount END) AS rev_2024,
    SUM(CASE WHEN d.year = 2025 THEN o.amount END) AS rev_2025,
    SUM(CASE WHEN d.year = 2025 THEN o.amount END) /
    NULLIF(SUM(CASE WHEN d.year = 2024 THEN o.amount END), 0) - 1 AS yoy_pct
FROM fct_orders o
JOIN dim_date d USING (date_id)
GROUP BY d.month_number, d.month_name
ORDER BY d.month_number;

    d.holiday_name,
    SUM(o.amount) AS holiday_revenue
FROM fct_orders o
JOIN dim_date d USING (date_id)
WHERE d.is_holiday = true
GROUP BY d.holiday_name
ORDER BY 2 DESC;
◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • dim_date is the most-used dimension; build it well
  • One row per date; 30-50+ attributes for filtering and grouping
  • Use dbt_utils.date_spine or dbt_date.get_date_dimension
  • Range: from before earliest fact data to 5+ years future
  • Include fiscal calendar columns if business uses non-calendar year
  • Holiday flags enable powerful seasonal/cyclical analysis
  • Multi-country businesses need per-country holiday flags
  • One canonical dim_date; role-play it as needed for different date roles

Date dimension across timezones: two sane designs — ONE date dimension in UTC (convert at query time), or multiple role-playing date dimensions per timezone. Pick one and document it; mixing silently is the bug.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Classic Kimball is 30+ years old. Modern columnar warehouses changed the math: storage is cheap, joins are slow, scans are fast. Some teams now skip star schemas entirely and use "One Big Table" patterns. Knowing when OBT beats star (and when it doesn't) makes you a smarter modeler.

One Big Table (OBT) defined

Instead of building a star schema, build a single wide denormalized table containing all the dimensions inline as columns:

# Star schema:
fct_orders + dim_customers + dim_products + dim_date
(JOIN to get full context)

# OBT equivalent:
big_orders:
| order_id | customer_id | customer_name | customer_segment | customer_country |
|          | product_id | product_name | product_category | product_brand     |
|          | order_date | year | quarter | month | day_of_week |
|          | amount | quantity | discount |
... 50-100+ columns

# Query: zero JOINs
SELECT customer_segment, SUM(amount)
FROM big_orders 
WHERE year = 2025
GROUP BY customer_segment;

Why OBT became viable

Three things changed:

  1. Columnar storage — Snowflake/BigQuery/Databricks scan only the columns you select; storage cost is per-column, not per-row
  2. Compression — duplicated values compress to nearly nothing in columnar formats
  3. Storage cost collapsed — $20/TB/month makes "store the dim columns inline" trivially affordable

OBT vs Star performance

Star OBT
Query simplicity Requires JOINs ✓ No JOINs
Query performance Hash JOINs (fast but extra step) ✓ Pure scan
Storage cost ✓ Lower (no duplication) Higher (denormalized)
Update cost ✓ Dim update touches few rows Dim update propagates to all facts
BI tool friendliness Semantic models nicely ✓ Simpler for ad-hoc SQL
Schema evolution ✓ Add to dim once Rebuild whole OBT
Drill-across ✓ Multiple facts via shared dims Hard — different OBTs duplicate dims

When OBT wins

  • Read-heavy ad-hoc queries — analysts running varied questions; JOIN cost adds up
  • Self-service BI — non-SQL users find OBT easier (one table, all columns)
  • Stable dimensions — customer attributes don't change often
  • Single domain analysis — most queries focused on orders, not cross-domain
  • Looker / Cube / dbt Semantic Layer — semantic layer generates SQL on top of OBT

When star wins

  • Multiple fact tables sharing dimensions — galaxy schema, drill-across critical
  • Dimensions change frequently — propagating to facts is expensive
  • Heavy SCD2 usage — version explosion in OBT is painful
  • Complex business logic — separation makes intermediate steps clearer
  • BI tool requires star — older BI tools may need explicit dim/fact

The hybrid pattern (most common)

Many teams now do:

  1. Build proper star schema as the core model (dim_customers, dim_products, fct_orders)
  2. Build OBT marts as consumption layer for specific use cases (big_orders_for_analysts, big_marketing_attribution)
# models/marts/fct_orders.sql        (star fact)
# models/marts/dim_customers.sql      (star dim, SCD2)
# models/marts/dim_products.sql       (star dim)
# models/marts/dim_date.sql           (conformed)

# models/marts/obt/obt_orders.sql     (consumption layer)
select
    o.order_id,
    o.order_date,
    -- denorm customer
    c.customer_name, c.customer_segment, c.customer_country,
    -- denorm product
    p.product_name, p.product_category, p.product_brand,
    -- denorm date
    d.year, d.quarter, d.month, d.is_holiday,
    -- measures
    o.amount, o.quantity, o.discount
from {{ ref('fct_orders') }} o
left join {{ ref('dim_customers') }} c using (customer_sk)
left join {{ ref('dim_products') }} p using (product_sk)
left join {{ ref('dim_date') }} d on o.order_date_id = d.date_id

# OBT is now derived from your clean star.
# Analysts query OBT; engineers maintain the star underneath.

OBT column-naming conventions

When everything is in one table, naming matters more than ever to keep columns navigable:

# Prefix related columns:
customer_id
customer_name
customer_segment
customer_country
customer_signup_date
...
product_id
product_name
product_category
product_brand
...
order_date
order_year
order_quarter
order_month
...

# Or use namespace::
order.id, order.date, order.amount
customer.id, customer.name, customer.segment
product.id, product.name, product.category

# Pick one convention; stick to it.

Refresh strategy

OBT rebuilds touch a lot of data:

  • Daily full refresh — simplest, works for <100M rows
  • Incremental on order_date — for large historical OBTs
  • Late-binding via views — query star at runtime; no materialized OBT
★ DON'T SKIP THE STAR

Even if your consumption is OBT, build the star first. Star schema is reusable, testable, and the source of truth. OBT is just a denormalized view on top. The "pure OBT" approach (skip dims entirely) tends to backfire as the warehouse grows.

▸ WORKED EXAMPLE — Sales reporting OBT
# Underlying star (built first):
# fct_orders, dim_customers, dim_products, dim_date

# OBT for sales team self-service:
# models/marts/obt/obt_sales.sql

select
    o.order_id,
    o.order_date,
    -- customer denorm
    c.customer_name, c.customer_segment, c.customer_country, c.is_premium,
    -- product denorm  
    p.product_name, p.product_category, p.product_brand, p.unit_cost,
    -- date denorm
    d.year, d.quarter, d.month, d.month_name, d.is_holiday, d.is_weekend,
    -- measures
    o.amount, o.quantity, o.discount,
    -- derived
    o.amount - (o.quantity * p.unit_cost) as gross_profit,
    (o.amount - (o.quantity * p.unit_cost)) / nullif(o.amount, 0) as gross_margin_pct
from {{ ref('fct_orders') }} o
left join {{ ref('dim_customers') }} c using (customer_sk)
left join {{ ref('dim_products') }} p using (product_sk)
left join {{ ref('dim_date') }} d on o.order_date_id = d.date_id

# Sales team queries:
SELECT customer_segment, SUM(gross_profit) 
FROM obt_sales 
WHERE year = 2025 GROUP BY 1;
# One table, no JOINs, instant.
◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Data Vault is the third major modeling paradigm (alongside Kimball and OBT). It's designed for enterprise data warehouses with auditable, scalable, source-flexible architecture. You won't use it daily, but you should know what it is — it appears at large enterprises, especially regulated industries.

Data Vault basics

Created by Dan Linstedt. Three core entity types:

THE THREE DATA VAULT ENTITIES
Hub: a list of unique business keys (one row per entity)
Link: a relationship between hubs (associations)
Satellite: descriptive attributes for hubs and links (history tracked)

Hubs

Each hub represents a business entity by its natural key. Minimal — just the key, surrogate hash, load date, source:

# hub_customer
| customer_hk         | customer_id  | load_date  | record_source |
| 'a7f3e2d9c8b1...'   | 'C42'        | 2025-05-15 | crm_system    |
| '5e9c4a2f8b3d...'   | 'C18'        | 2025-05-15 | crm_system    |

# hub_product
# hub_order
# hub_employee
# ... one hub per business concept

Links

Relationships between hubs. Captures associations as their own entity:

# link_customer_order
| customer_order_hk    | customer_hk        | order_hk         | load_date  |
| 'b8e4f3a1...'        | 'a7f3e2d9c8b1...'  | 'c9d2e7f5...'    | 2025-05-15 |

# Captures: this customer is associated with this order
# Many-to-many handled natively (just multiple link rows)

Satellites

All descriptive attributes live in satellites, with full history. Multiple satellites can hang off one hub or link.

# sat_customer_details (basic info)
| customer_hk         | load_date  | end_date   | name  | email           | source    |
| 'a7f3e2d9c8b1...'   | 2024-01-15 | 2025-04-15 | Alice | alice@old.com   | crm       |
| 'a7f3e2d9c8b1...'   | 2025-04-15 | NULL       | Alice | alice@new.com   | crm       |

# sat_customer_segment (separate concern)
| customer_hk         | load_date  | end_date   | segment    | source    |
| 'a7f3e2d9c8b1...'   | 2024-01-15 | 2025-04-15 | small_biz  | analytics |
| 'a7f3e2d9c8b1...'   | 2025-04-15 | NULL       | enterprise | analytics |

# Each satellite tracks history independently
# Sources can be different
# All have load_date/end_date for time-tracking

Why Data Vault?

Auditability Every value tracked with source + timestamp; full lineage
Source flexibility Add new sources without breaking existing models (new satellites)
Scalability Tables grow predictably; parallel load-friendly
Refactor resilience Source schema changes only affect one satellite
Regulatory friendly Banking, healthcare love the audit trail

The downsides

  • Complexity — many small tables (3-4× more tables than Kimball)
  • Query difficulty — analysts can't query DV directly; needs a presentation layer
  • Modeling overhead — significant upfront design
  • Tool support — less mainstream than Kimball; fewer dbt patterns

Typical architecture with Data Vault

Sources
   ↓
Raw Vault (DV: hubs, links, satellites — minimal transformation)
   ↓
Business Vault (DV-style but with computed/derived business logic)
   ↓
Information Marts (Kimball-style star schemas for consumption)
   ↓
BI tools / analysts

DV sits BELOW the star. Analysts query stars; DV is the storage/audit foundation.

When Data Vault fits

  • Large enterprise warehouses — 100s of sources, complex domain
  • Regulated industries — banking, healthcare, insurance, gov
  • Many sources changing independently — new sources frequently added
  • Strong audit requirements — every value traceable to source
  • Long-term warehouses — 10+ year lifespan with team churn

When NOT to use Data Vault

  • Small/medium warehouses — complexity overhead isn't worth it
  • Self-service analytics primary use case — DV is hostile to ad-hoc queries
  • Few sources / stable schemas — DV's flexibility isn't needed
  • Standard SaaS analytics — Kimball + dbt is plenty
★ FOR MOST DBT TEAMS

Don't use Data Vault. dbt's typical pattern (staging → intermediate → marts with Kimball star) is sufficient for 95% of analytics work. Reach for DV only if you're at a large enterprise with regulatory pressure and complex multi-source integration.

# Question: Customer's total revenue, by segment

# Kimball Star (3 tables):
SELECT c.segment, SUM(o.amount)
FROM fct_orders o
JOIN dim_customers c USING (customer_sk)
GROUP BY c.segment;

# OBT (1 table):
SELECT customer_segment, SUM(amount)
FROM obt_orders
GROUP BY customer_segment;

# Data Vault (5+ tables, complex):
SELECT cs.segment, SUM(os.amount)
FROM hub_customer hc
JOIN sat_customer_segment cs 
  ON hc.customer_hk = cs.customer_hk AND cs.end_date IS NULL
JOIN link_customer_order lco USING (customer_hk)
JOIN hub_order ho ON lco.order_hk = ho.order_hk
JOIN sat_order_amount os 
  ON ho.order_hk = os.order_hk AND os.end_date IS NULL
GROUP BY cs.segment;

# This is why DV needs a presentation layer (star/OBT) on top.
◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Data Vault: Hubs (entities), Links (relationships), Satellites (attributes with history)
  • Designed for enterprise warehouses with audit and source-flexibility requirements
  • Strengths: auditable, scalable, source-flexible, refactor-resilient
  • Weaknesses: complex, query-hostile, requires presentation layer on top
  • Typical pattern: DV underneath, Kimball star marts on top for consumption
  • Use for: large regulated enterprises with many evolving sources
  • For most dbt teams: stick with Kimball + dbt. DV is overkill.

Data Vault keys: DV uses HASH keys (MD5/SHA of the business key) for join performance and cross-system stability — hubs, links, and satellites all key on those hashes.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

The biggest analytics pain point at most companies: the same metric calculated differently in different places. "Revenue" means three things across three dashboards. Metric layers (semantic layers) solve this by defining metrics once, in a central spec, that all consumers reference. They're rapidly becoming the new modeling frontier.

The metric inconsistency problem

Without a metric layer:

# Sales dashboard (in Tableau):
revenue = SUM(amount) WHERE status = 'completed'

# Finance dashboard (in Looker):
revenue = SUM(amount - discount) WHERE status IN ('completed', 'shipped')

# Marketing dashboard (in Power BI):
revenue = SUM(amount) WHERE order_date >= signup_date - 7

# All three report different numbers for "revenue last month"
# Every meeting becomes "whose number is right?"

What a metric layer does

Define metrics once in code. All BI tools reference the central definition.

METRIC LAYER PRINCIPLES
1. Single definition — revenue defined in one file
2. Centrally versioned — under source control, reviewed via PR
3. Tool-agnostic — Tableau, Looker, Power BI all read it
4. Composable — metrics build on metrics (gross_margin = revenue - cogs)

Major metric layer products

dbt Semantic Layer (MetricFlow) Built into dbt; define metrics in YAML; query via SQL or API
Cube Open-source semantic layer; works with any warehouse
LookML (Looker) First mainstream metric layer; tied to Looker BI tool
Lightdash Open-source; reads dbt metric definitions
Hex / Mode / Sigma Modern BI tools with built-in semantic capabilities

dbt Semantic Layer example

# models/semantic_models/orders.yml

semantic_models:
  - name: orders
    description: Order events
    model: ref('fct_orders')
    
    entities:
      - name: order
        type: primary
        expr: order_id
      - name: customer
        type: foreign
        expr: customer_id
    
    dimensions:
      - name: order_date
        type: time
        expr: order_date
        type_params:
          time_granularity: day
      - name: status
        type: categorical
        expr: status
    
    measures:
      - name: revenue
        description: Gross order amount (before discounts)
        expr: amount
        agg: sum
      - name: discount
        expr: discount_amount
        agg: sum
      - name: order_count
        expr: order_id
        agg: count_distinct

metrics:
  - name: revenue
    label: Revenue
    description: Total order revenue
    type: simple
    type_params:
      measure: revenue
    filter: "{{ Dimension('order__status') }} = 'completed'"
  
  - name: net_revenue
    label: Net Revenue
    type: derived
    type_params:
      expr: "revenue - discount"
      metrics:
        - name: revenue
        - name: discount

Querying through the semantic layer

# dbt sl query (CLI)
dbt sl query   --metrics revenue,net_revenue   --group-by order_date__month,customer__segment   --where "order_date__month >= '2025-01-01'"

# Or via SQL using semantic layer:
SELECT * FROM {{ semantic_layer.query(
    metrics=['revenue', 'net_revenue'],
    group_by=['metric_time__month', 'customer__segment']
) }}

# The semantic layer generates the SQL automatically with consistent definitions

Why metric layers are taking over

  1. Eliminates definition drift — one source of truth
  2. Version control — metric changes go through PR review
  3. Tool flexibility — switch BI tools without re-defining metrics
  4. Self-service — analysts pick from defined metrics rather than write SQL
  5. Lineage — see which dashboards depend on which metrics

The downsides

  • Setup cost — defining all metrics formally takes time
  • Learning curve — new YAML schema and concepts
  • Tool support — your BI tool needs to integrate (varies)
  • Maturity — dbt Semantic Layer is still evolving

Implementing in stages

You don't need a full semantic layer day one. Progress in stages:

  1. Stage 1: Document metric definitions in a wiki / Confluence
  2. Stage 2: Centralize KPI calculations in a single dbt model (fct_metrics_monthly)
  3. Stage 3: Adopt dbt Semantic Layer for the most-disputed metrics
  4. Stage 4: Roll out to all metrics; sunset duplicate definitions in BI tools

Avoiding metric drift

Three techniques that help even without a full semantic layer:

# 1. Macros for repeated calculations
# macros/revenue_definition.sql
{% macro net_revenue(amount_col, discount_col) %}
    sum({{ amount_col }}) - coalesce(sum({{ discount_col }}), 0)
{% endmacro %}

# Now use everywhere:
select customer_id, {{ net_revenue('amount', 'discount') }} as net_revenue
from fct_orders
group by 1;

# 2. Centralized metric marts
# models/marts/metrics/fct_monthly_kpis.sql
# One row per (month, segment) with ALL KPIs pre-calculated
# All BI tools read THIS, not raw data

# 3. Tested business rules in dbt
# tests/revenue_consistency.sql
SELECT *
FROM (
    SELECT 'finance' AS source, SUM(net_revenue) FROM fct_monthly_kpis
    UNION ALL
    SELECT 'sales' AS source, SUM(net_revenue) FROM sales_summary
)
HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT amount) > 1   -- fails if sources disagree

# Company has 6 different "revenue" definitions across tools
# Goal: one definition, all tools

# Phase 1 (week 1): audit
# - Interview each team
# - Document existing definitions
# - Identify the "true" canonical version (often finance owns it)

# Phase 2 (weeks 2-3): build canonical metric in dbt
# semantic_models/revenue.yml defines THE definition
# - Filters: order_status IN ('completed', 'shipped')  
# - Components: amount - discount - refund_amount

# Phase 3 (weeks 4-6): rollout
# - Update Tableau workbooks to query semantic layer
# - Update Looker to use the same dbt source
# - Update finance Excel models

# Phase 4 (ongoing): governance
# - Any metric change goes through PR
# - Reviewed by data team + business owner
# - Auto-tests prevent drift

# Result: one number in every meeting. The wars are over.
◇ KEY TAKEAWAYS
  • Metric layer = centralized metric definitions referenced by all consumers
  • Solves the "same metric, different values" problem
  • Major options: dbt Semantic Layer (MetricFlow), Cube, LookML, Lightdash
  • Define metrics in YAML; query via SQL or API
  • Benefits: consistency, version control, tool flexibility, lineage
  • Cost: setup time + learning curve + tool maturity
  • Even without a formal layer: dbt macros + centralized metric marts help
  • Roll out in stages — pick most-disputed metrics first
