◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

You'll inherit bad models; you'll review teammates' PRs; you'll occasionally need to redesign existing models. A solid checklist for "is this model healthy?" speeds up reviews and catches the patterns that cause downstream pain. This is the practical capstone of modeling.

The model review checklist

Run through these questions for any new or modified data model:

QUALITY DIMENSIONS
1. Grain — is it declared and consistent?
2. Keys — are primary/foreign keys defined and tested?
3. Layer adherence — staging/intermediate/marts respected?
4. Documentation — descriptions present?
5. Tests — unique, not_null, relationships at minimum?
6. Naming — conventions followed?
7. Materialization — appropriate choice (view/table/incremental)?
8. Performance — sensible at expected volume?
9. Lineage — uses ref() and source()?
10. Business logic — correctly placed (intermediate, not staging)?

1. Grain

# ✓ Good
description: |
  One row per order. order_id is unique.

# ✗ Bad
description: |
  Order data.   # what does one row mean? Per order? Per item? Per shipment?

2. Keys

# ✓ Good — surrogate key + tests
columns:
  - name: order_sk
    description: Surrogate primary key
    tests: [unique, not_null]
  - name: order_id  
    description: Natural key from source
    tests: [unique, not_null]
  - name: customer_sk
    description: FK to dim_customers
    tests:
      - not_null
      - relationships:
          to: ref('dim_customers')
          field: customer_sk

# ✗ Bad — no tests, no clear PK
columns:
  - name: id
  - name: customer_id
# Reviewers can't trust the data without tests

3. Layer adherence

# ✓ Good — staging is simple
-- models/staging/stg_app__orders.sql
select
    id as order_id,
    customer_id,
    amount::numeric / 100 as amount_usd,
    created_at::timestamp as created_at
from {{ source('app', 'orders') }}

# ✗ Bad — business logic in staging
-- models/staging/stg_app__orders.sql
select
    o.id as order_id,
    o.customer_id,
    c.segment,                              -- ❌ JOIN in staging
    case when o.amount > 1000 then 'high' end as size_tier,  -- ❌ logic in staging
    o.amount / 100 as amount_usd
from {{ source('app', 'orders') }} o
join {{ source('app', 'customers') }} c using (customer_id)
where o.status = 'completed'                -- ❌ business filter in staging

4. Documentation

# ✓ Good
- name: fct_orders
  description: |
    Order-level fact table.
    Grain: one row per order.
    Source: app.orders (PostgreSQL).
    Updated daily at 3am UTC.
  columns:
    - name: amount_usd
      description: |
        Total order amount in USD. ADDITIVE.
        Includes discounts; excludes tax and shipping.

# ✗ Bad
- name: fct_orders
  description: Orders fact
  columns:
    - name: amount_usd
      description: Amount  # what unit? what about tax?

5. Tests

# Minimum tests for every fact/dim:
columns:
  - name: <primary_key>
    tests: [unique, not_null]
  - name: <foreign_key>
    tests:
      - not_null
      - relationships:
          to: ref('dim_X')
          field: X_sk
  - name: <enum_column>
    tests:
      - accepted_values:
          values: ['low', 'medium', 'high']

# Don't skip these. PRs without tests should be blocked.

6. Naming conventions

# Standard dbt naming:
stg_<source>__<entity>     -- stg_stripe__charges
int_<area>_<purpose>        -- int_orders_with_refunds
fct_<event>                  -- fct_orders, fct_page_views
dim_<entity>                 -- dim_customers, dim_products

# Column conventions:
-- snake_case
-- descriptive
-- consistent units in name when ambiguous (amount_usd, duration_sec)
-- IDs: <entity>_id (natural), <entity>_sk (surrogate)
-- Booleans: is_X, has_X
-- Timestamps: X_at (created_at), X_ts (event_ts)
-- Dates: X_date (signup_date)

7. Materialization choice

Materialization Use for
view Small data, frequently changing logic, cheap to recompute
table Larger data, queried often, full refresh acceptable
incremental Large append-only tables (events, orders); refresh slows otherwise
ephemeral Intermediate models with logic, no need to materialize

8. Performance check

# Red flags:
# - JOINs without ON clauses (Cartesian!)
# - SELECT * on a 100-col source
# - Window functions on un-partitioned huge tables
# - SUBQUERY in WHERE for each row (correlated)
# - Multiple full scans when one would suffice

# Quick check: how long does dbt run --select model take?
# <1 min: probably fine
# 1-10 min: review for optimization
# >10 min: definitely needs work (clustering, incremental, restructure)

9. Lineage hygiene

# ✓ Good — uses ref() and source()
from {{ ref('stg_orders') }}
join {{ ref('dim_customers') }} using (customer_sk)
left join {{ source('crm', 'leads') }} on ...

# ✗ Bad — hardcoded names
from raw_data.staged_orders
join analytics.dim_customers using (customer_sk)
# Breaks lineage; env-specific; fragile

10. Business logic placement

Logic type Belongs in
Column renames, casts Staging
Source filtering (e.g., remove test data) Staging (with comment why)
JOINs, complex derivations Intermediate
Business rules (status, segments) Intermediate or marts
Final denormalization Marts
Pre-aggregated KPIs Marts (downstream of dims/facts)

Refactoring a broken model

You inherited a model. It's slow, untested, undocumented. What do you do?

  1. Document current behavior first — write tests that pass against current state. These become your safety net.
  2. Identify the grain — write it down. If unclear, that's bug #1.
  3. Add layer separation — extract staging if it's all in one model.
  4. Add key tests — unique on grain key, not_null on FKs.
  5. Refactor in slices — one logical chunk at a time, with tests as guardrails.
  6. Run side-by-side — keep the old version; build the new one; compare outputs row-by-row.
  7. Swap once verified — switch downstream consumers; deprecate old.

# 2. Keys: ✓ event_sk unique + not_null. customer_sk FK with relationships test.
# 3. Layer: ✓ References stg_app__subscription_events and int_customer_status
# 4. Docs: ✓ Description present, all columns described, units specified
# 5. Tests: ✓ Unique, not_null, relationships, accepted_values on event_type
# 6. Naming: ✓ fct_ prefix, snake_case columns
# 7. Materialization: ✓ Incremental on event_date — appropriate for append-only
# 8. Performance: ~ JOIN on int_customer_status not filtered first; might be slow at scale

  • Most bugs come from skipping grain declaration or layer violations
  • Refactor inherited models incrementally with tests as guardrails
  • Run new vs old side-by-side before swapping consumers
  • This checklist applies whether you wrote the model or are reviewing it
  • Building habits around these 10 = long-term warehouse health

🧠 The Aistote Method (J-Method)

THE IDEA
The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its "J-Method"). Instead of slowly re-reading, you spend the time testing yourself and re-testing what you miss. This app already has every tool the method needs.

SCD Types: 0, 1, 2, 3

The SCD problem — When a dimension's attribute changes, what do you do? Three main strategies:

SCD Type 0 — Retain Original — The original value never changes, even if the source updates. Used for unchanging facts about an entity.

SCD Type 1 — Overwrite — The most common: just update the row with the latest value. No history retained.

SCD Type 2 — Add New Row — The powerhouse. When an attribute changes, you insert a new row with a new effective date range. The old row's valid_to closes; a new row opens.

SCD Type 3 — Add New Column — Track just the previous value alongside the current. Limited history but no row explosion.
